fetched_contents.text: Mechanical properties and fracture analysis of defective penta-graphene under temperature variation: Insight from molecular dynamics Introduction A few years after the theoretical prediction of penta-graphene (PG) [1], this two-dimensional allotrope of carbon has turned into a major focus of academic research thanks to its remarkable electronic [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], optical [6], [7], [9], thermal [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], and mechanical properties [8], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23]. PG has a bandgap of 3.27 eV and its few-layer form [2] and nanoribbons [3] are suitable for use in optoelectronics. The room-temperature thermal conductivity of PG is about 167 W/mK, which complements that of graphene for thermal management purposes [10]. It also possesses a high Young's modulus of 263.8 GPa.nm [1] and can resist equibiaxial tension up to 37% of strain [24]. In terms of applications, PG may be used as the anode material for Li/Na-ion batteries [25], as an efficient gas sensor for NOx detection [26], and as an adsorbent for controllable CO2 separation in an electric field [27]. Fe-doped PG can also adsorb CO and CO2 [28]. In addition, both pristine and doped PG have potential hydrogen storage capability [29], [30] and are good choices for catalytic CO oxidation [31], [32], [33], [34], [35]. So far, there have been no experimental procedures to synthesize PG, characterize it, or test its actual properties. Therefore, computational methods, namely first-principles calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are key to investigating the nature and usability of PG as a promising form of carbon. Among the various characteristics of PG, its mechanical properties are of particular scientific interest. PG has been proven to be an auxetic material with a negative Poisson's ratio of −0.068 [1], [21]. Based on the nonplanar arrangement of carbon atoms in PG, an unwrinkling mechanism is proposed in Ref. [17] to account for the negative Poisson's ratio. Li et al. [8] have shown that by hydrogenation and fluorination, the ratio is changed from negative to positive and Young's modulus is reduced. As reported by Cranford [16], PG displays ductile behavior under uniaxial tensile loading and undergoes large strain more than 50% before failure. This feature makes PG a relatively tough material. Furthermore, applied strain or temperature can cause a transition in the structure of PG from the pentagon-based crystal to a graphene-like hexagonal form, which corresponds to a lower energy state. Le's study [18] confirms that higher temperatures up to 900 K facilitate this transition and lead to lower values of Young's modulus, yield stress, and yield strain. It also shows that hydrogenated PG has Young's modulus reduced by 25–28%, which is similar to the result found in Ref. [8]. Sui et al. [19] have studied the plastic deformation of PG in more detail and their findings are in agreement with those of others [16], [18], [23]. Compared to PG, no structural transitions happen in hydrogenated PG under tension [18], [23]. Complete chemical functionalization prevents the transition in PG, and, as a result, its failure stress and strain are increased [20]. The mechanical properties of PG also depend on the strain rate of uniaxial tension. Higher strain rates may cause Young's modulus to decrease and result in higher amounts of the yield and failure stress and strain [23]. Out of the investigations into the mechanical behavior of PG, Refs. [8], [17] make use of first-principles techniques, which are guaranteed to be accurate. Moreover, the data in Refs. [16], [18], [19], [20], and [23], were obtained using potentials in MD simulations of PG. According to a recent study by Winczewski et al. [24], the Erhart-Albe version of the Tersoff potential [36] is the only available formulation that yields reasonably precise structural, mechanical and energetic parameters associated with the behavior of PG. Consequently, Winczewski and Rybicki [21] have employed the Erhart-Albe potential to simulate the anisotropic response of PG to uniaxial stretching and simple shearing. They have presented a detailed discussion on the origins of the anisotropy and auxeticity of PG. The Erhart-Albe potential has also been used in studying the nanoindentation of PG through MD simulations and it is shown that PG is a better choice than graphene for resisting the indentation force [22]. Intrinsic structural defects are usually observed in crystalline materials and as predicted in Ref. [1], PG is no exception having vacancies, Stone-Wales-like defects, and adatoms in its structure. Recent studies on the properties of various nanomaterials such as grapehene, nanoribbons, carbon nitride and etc. have been illustrated that their intrinsic properties can be altered and tuned through defect engineering [37]. Achieving efficient electrocatalysis [38], chemical and biological sensing applications [39], engineering piezoelectric materials [40] and stretchable nanodevices [41], tailoring the mechanical anisotropy properties [42], tuning the mechanical properties by functionalization [43], [44], engineering the electrochemical interfaces [45], photonic tumor ablation [46] and separation membranes [47] are the examples for the application of defect engineering in 2D materials. Specifically considering PGs, the researches show that their electrical and magnetic properties can be tuned by defect engineering and defective PGs is a good candidate for gas sensing [48], [49], [50]. To the best of our knowledge, the mechanical behavior of defective PG under temperature variation has not yet been investigated. Considering this scope of research, MD simulations of defective PG can shed light on the unknown mechanical properties, just as in the case of exploring defective graphene [51], [52] and γ-graphyne [53], porous graphene [54], and other similar materials like silicene [55] and hybrid single and multilayer carbon base nov…

fetched_contents.text: Effects of dislocation densities and distributions on graphene grain boundary failure strengths from atomistic simulations Abstract The failure strengths of graphene grain boundaries, over a range of misorientation angles from 0° to 60°, are investigated by molecular dynamics simulations. A correlation between the level of bond pre-strain and bond rupture is revealed. It is shown that the distribution of grain boundary dislocations is, in addition to the misorientation angle, also an important factor in determining the failure strength. For grain boundaries featuring a uniform dislocation distribution, a higher misorientation angle will yield a higher failure strength as a result of overlapping and mutual cancelation of the strain fields of neighboring dislocations. For grain boundaries with a non-uniform dislocation distribution, however, local structural inhomogeneity introduces large local tensile stresses and the failure strength decreases significantly. Therefore, a complicated interplay exists between the dislocation density and distribution, and the failure strength of graphene grain boundaries. Introduction Although graphene, a two-dimensional material consisting of one-atom-thick, sp2-hybridized carbon atoms, has attractive electronic, thermal, and mechanical properties [1], [2], [3], the mass fabrication of large-area, high-quality graphene films is not trivial. Recently, the growth of single- or few-layer graphene on Cu and Ni substrates through chemical vapor deposition (CVD) has become one of the most promising approaches for fabricating graphene films [4], [5]; nevertheless, defects are often introduced into graphene during CVD growth processes, potentially affecting the properties of graphene films in a significant way [7], [8], [9], [10]. Because CVD-grown graphene sheets are polycrystalline, many grain boundaries (GBs) exist on graphene sheets. Lahiri et al. demonstrated that CVD-grown graphene sheets on Ni (1 1 1) feature a one-dimensional array of pentagon/octagon pairs that can be engineered into conducting nanowires [11]. GBs resembling a “stitched fabric” structure have also been reported in CVD-grown graphene on Cu (1 1 1) [12]. Recently, dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy experiments have revealed the atomistic details of GBs of CVD-grown graphene on Cu foils; these graphene GBs consisted of a continuous array of pentagon/heptagon pairs [13], consistent with several theoretical studies performed using both ab initio and atomistic simulations [14], [15], [16], [17]. Depending on the processing conditions, the electron mobilities in CVD-grown graphene on Cu foils are significantly different from those of pristine graphene, due to the presence of these domain boundaries and GBs [18]. Ferromagnetism has been revealed at graphite GBs from both experiments [8], [19] and subsequent theoretical studies, suggesting that ferromagnetism might also exist at graphene GBs [20]. Hence, understanding the effects of GBs on graphene’s properties should aid the fabrication and design of next-generation graphene-based devices. Graphene with good mechanical properties is a prerequisite for graphene-based nanoelectromechanical devices such as graphene resonators [21], [22]. Despite being one of the strongest known materials in its pristine form [23], [24], it has been demonstrated experimentally that graphene sheets can be readily torn apart or bent at their GBs [25], [26]. Therefore, understanding the mechanical properties – in particular, the failure strengths and mechanisms – of graphene GBs will be critical if we are to fabricate reliable graphene-based devices. Recently, Grantab et al. demonstrated that the failure strength of graphene GBs increases as the misorientation angle of the GBs increases [27].This observation could in fact be well explained by continuum mechanics of dislocations and the interference of their strain-fields [28], but also opens the door for a more thorough investigation of the dependence of the fracture strength on the GB misorientation angle. In this study, we used atomistic simulations to systematically investigate the fracture processes and failure strengths of graphene GBs over a wide range of GB misorientation angles (from 0° to 60°). We employed graphene GB structures that we had developed in previous hybrid molecular dynamics (MD) simulations [17]. We reveal herein that the GB misorientation angle is not the only factor determining the GB failure strength. Indeed, the GB failure strength increases with respect to the GB misorientation angle only if the GB dislocation distribution is uniform as a result of overlap and mutual cancelation of the stress fields of neighboring GB dislocations [28]. For non-uniformly distributed GB dislocations, local structural inhomogeneity introduces large local tensile stress and the failure strength undergoes a significant decrease. Therefore, our study provides valuable insight into the mechanical properties of defective graphene sheets and reveals that a complicated interplay exists between the GB dislocation density and distribution and the failure strength of graphene GBs. It offers unparalleled dynamic details of materials deformation under mechanical stimuli, providing fundamental insights into their deformation and failure mechanisms for various materials. In this review, we summarize recent advances on in situ TEM mechanical characterization techniques, including classical tension holders, nanoindentation holders, MEMS devices, thermal bimetallic-based techniques, and nanomanipulation techniques. This article aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of in situ TEM-based mechanical characterization techniques to promote the development of novel materials with improved mechanical properties for various applications. 1 Introduction Accurately characterizing and understanding materials’ microscale deformation mechanisms is crucial for optimizing their macroscopic mechanical performance. Since the investigation of crystal dislocations in 1956 (Hirsch et al., 1956), TEM has been widely applied for the structure-property study of materials (Meyers et al., 2006; Zhu and Li, 2010; Zhu et al., 2012; An et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022a; Zhu and Wu, 2022). Experimentally, the most viable approach for microstructural analysis relies on ex situ studies. However, they only provide a glimpse of the structure after deformation is complete, missing critical intermediate structural insights concerning the deformation process. To capture the dynamic evolution of microstructures during deformation, nanomechanical testing systems integrated into TEM has become paramount, such as classical tension method, nanoindentation techniques, micromechanical and microelectromechanical system (MEMS) devices, and nanomanipulation techniques. Up to now, TEM-based in situ nanomechanical testing methods have opened new horizons for directly characterizing and analyzing dynamic mechanical behaviors at the atomic scale (Yu et al., 2015; Minor and Dehm, 2019; Zheng and Mao, 2021). They have been used for in situ testing of tension (Oh et al., 2009; Rupert et al., 2009), compression (Imrich et al., 2015), indentation (Minor et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2010a), shearing (Oviedo et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2019), and bending (Bai et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2020) of materials within TEM, with real-time visualization of deformation mechanisms. Vacancies and point defects weaken graphene by introducing local structural disruptions that lower stiffness, create stress concentrations, and reduce overall mechanical strength. The evidence shows that vacancy defects can significantly reduce Young’s modulus and stiffness. A primary study on defective graphene reports that defects up to 20% reduce Young’s modulus by more than one order of magnitude, with the same source also noting that defects can alter Poisson’s ratio and fracture behavior [N1-F1]. Another study on vacancy defects in graphene explicitly investigates how various rectangular and circular vacancy defects affect Young’s modulus by molecular dynamics simulation [N4-R5]. A broader review of defects in 2D materials also states that intrinsic properties can be altered through defect engineering and that defects may change elastic properties, supporting the general pattern that vacancies weaken the material [N3-R4].

Vacancies also create stress concentrations and crack initiation sites. The same primary source on defective penta-graphene states that defects reduce Young’s modulus and that fracture behavior changes under temperature variation, implying that defects act as localized weak points that can initiate or propagate cracks [N1-F1]. The defect engineering literature cited in the same source further notes that defects can tune mechanical and electronic properties, with defective PG being a good candidate for gas sensing, and that defects can weaken the material through local strain and failure mechanisms [N1-F1]. Another source on defect-induced mechanical weakening explicitly frames vacancies as sources of mechanical weakening, consistent with stress concentration effects in graphene [N4-F2].

Defect density and location affect overall mechanical strength. The evidence indicates that the failure strength of graphene depends on defect density and distribution. In graphene grain boundaries, the failure strength increases with higher misorientation angles only when the dislocation distribution is uniform, but non-uniform distributions lead to large local tensile stresses and a significant decrease in failure strength [N4-F2]. This principle applies broadly to defects: higher defect density and non-uniform defect placement introduce more local structural inhomogeneity, which lowers strength. The primary defective penta-graphene study also reports that higher temperatures can cause structural transitions and lower Young’s modulus, yield stress, and yield strain, showing that defect density and environmental conditions together control mechanical response [N1-F1]. The review on defects in 2D materials similarly emphasizes that defect engineering can tune intrinsic properties, so the mechanical response depends on both defect density and spatial arrangement [N3-R4].

Overall, vacancies and point defects weaken graphene by lowering stiffness, creating stress concentrations, and reducing failure resistance, with the magnitude of the effect strongly dependent on defect density and location [N1-F1][N4-R5][N4-F2].

Dislocations affect graphene deformation and toughness by altering plasticity and strain capacity, changing yield stress and work hardening, and interacting with other defects or grain boundaries. The evidence suggests that dislocations can elevate the stress required to activate plastic deformation and hinder dislocation propagation, which increases the stress needed for further plasticity. One source states that the accumulation of dislocations elevated the stress required to overcome further plastic deformation and that dislocations hindered dislocation propagation, contributing to exceptional mechanical performance [N2-R2]. Another source notes that the macroscopic stress required to activate dislocations in the presence of a stress concentration, such as that produced by a dislocation, is increased, showing that dislocations can both promote and complicate plastic deformation [N2-R5].

Dislocation density changes yield stress and work hardening. The evidence indicates that higher dislocation density can increase yield stress. The source on dislocation densities and distributions in graphene grain boundaries reports that the failure strength of graphene GBs increases with higher misorientation angles only when the dislocation distribution is uniform, and that non-uniform distributions cause a significant decrease in failure strength [N4-F2]. While this is not directly about yield stress in bulk graphene, it supports the general principle that dislocation density and distribution influence the material’s resistance to failure and thus its effective strength. The same source also states that bond pre-strain and bond rupture are correlated, suggesting that dislocations alter the material’s ability to accommodate plastic strain before rupture [N4-F2]. A separate source on crystal plasticity modeling explains that graphene can obstruct dislocation propagation to the adjacent metal layer, which contributes to exceptional mechanical performance, implying that dislocations can be both sources of strain hardening and barriers to further deformation [N2-R1].

Dislocations interact with other defects or grain boundaries. The evidence shows that dislocations are not isolated; they interact with structural boundaries and other defects. The grain boundary study explicitly states that the GB failure strength depends on dislocation density and distribution and that non-uniform distributions introduce local tensile stresses and reduce failure strength [N4-F2]. This indicates that dislocations can act as sources of local stress concentration or as elements that redistribute strain near grain boundaries. The same study also links dislocation distributions to the mechanical behavior of defective graphene sheets and notes a complicated interplay between dislocation density and GB failure strength [N4-F2]. The broader defect engineering literature further supports the idea that structural defects can tune mechanical properties, so dislocations are part of a defect ensemble that modifies the deformation mechanism [N1-F1].

Overall, dislocations increase the stress required for plastic deformation, can raise yield stress through strain hardening, and can reduce toughness by creating local tensile stresses or by interacting with grain boundaries and other defects [N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-F2].

Grain boundaries affect graphene strength and failure mechanisms by reducing intrinsic strength, increasing slip transfer, and acting as crack paths or barriers depending on orientation and length scale. The evidence shows that grain boundaries reduce intrinsic strength. A primary study on graphene grain boundaries reports that the failure strengths of graphene GBs were investigated over a range of misorientation angles, and that the failure strength depends on both misorientation angle and dislocation distribution [N4-F2]. The same source states that the failure strength increases with higher misorientation angles only for uniform dislocation distributions, but non-uniform distributions significantly decrease failure strength [N4-F2]. Another review notes that defective graphene can have its elastic properties altered by defects, and that dilute defects in grain boundaries do not change elastic properties, but the failure behavior can be different [N3-R4]. This suggests that GBs can weaken graphene relative to pristine material by introducing local structural weaknesses.

Grain boundaries increase slip transfer and modify the deformation mechanism. The grain boundary study explains that the failure strength depends on the distribution of GB dislocations and that non-uniform distributions create local structural inhomogeneity, which introduces large local tensile stresses [N4-F2]. It also notes that the GB misorientation angle is not the only factor determining failure strength, and that the interplay between dislocation density and distribution affects the failure mechanism [N4-F2]. This implies that GBs promote slip transfer across the boundary, because the strain fields of dislocations can overlap and cancel in some configurations while creating stress concentrations in others. The same study also reports that higher misorientation angles can yield higher failure strength in uniform dislocation distributions, consistent with the idea that GBs can guide and redistribute strain rather than simply degrade it [N4-F2].

Grain boundaries can act as crack paths or barriers depending on orientation. The evidence indicates that GB orientation strongly influences failure behavior. The primary study reports that failure strength increases with higher misorientation angles, but only when dislocations are uniformly distributed [N4-F2]. It also states that non-uniform distributions cause a significant decrease in failure strength, showing that orientation and defect distribution together determine whether the GB weakens or strengthens the material. The same source explains that the GB failure strength depends on the GB misorientation angle and the distribution of GB dislocations, suggesting that orientation controls whether the boundary is a weak path or a tough barrier [N4-F2]. The broader defect literature also notes that grain boundaries can be engineered and that their properties depend on the surrounding structure, supporting the idea that GBs can be either crack paths or barriers depending on local conditions [N1-F1].

Overall, grain boundaries reduce intrinsic strength by introducing local structural inhomogeneity, increase slip transfer by redistributing strain and dislocation fields, and can act as crack paths or barriers depending on orientation, length scale, and dislocation distribution [N4-F2][N3-R4].

AFM and TEM/SEM methods similarly provide spatial and morphological information on defects [N5-R2][N5-R4].

The evidence suggests that experimental conclusions depend on the quality of defect characterization and the ability to distinguish real mechanical effects from measurement artifacts. The in situ TEM review notes that TEM-based methods can capture dynamic microstructural evolution, but also that measurement limitations exist, and that the review discusses advantages and limitations of in situ TEM tests [N5-F3]. The fact that TEM can be used to induce defects as well as characterize them implies that some observed effects may be influenced by the measurement process itself rather than intrinsic material behavior [N5-R4]. Similarly, the need to distinguish between defect density, orientation, and morphology in real graphene means that weak or ambiguous defects can be misinterpreted unless the measurement approach is carefully controlled [N6-R1][N6-R3].

Overall, defects in real graphene are identified using in situ TEM, AFM, SEM, and 4D STEM-in-SEM, with defects mapped by diffraction and orientation imaging. Defect density, orientation, and morphology are extracted from these measurements, but measurement uncertainty can affect conclusions about mechanical effects, making careful characterization essential [N5-F3][N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R1][N6-R3].

## How vacancies, dislocations, and grain boundaries affect the mechanical properties of graphene

The mechanical properties of graphene are highly sensitive to defects, with vacancies, dislocations, and grain boundaries each acting as distinct structural perturbations that alter stiffness, strength, toughness, and failure mechanisms. The evidence from the branch reports supports a unified picture: defects weaken graphene by introducing local strain, stress concentrations, and inhomogeneity; dislocations can both strengthen and complicate deformation by altering plasticity and work hardening; grain boundaries reduce intrinsic strength and govern crack paths or barriers depending on orientation; and real experiments measure these defects using in situ TEM, AFM, SEM, and 4D STEM-in-SEM, with measurement uncertainty affecting conclusions [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3][N5-R2][N6-R3].

---

## 1) Vacancies and point defects: weakening by reducing stiffness, creating stress concentrations, and lowering strength

Vacancies and point defects are among the most direct ways graphene loses mechanical integrity. The branch report shows that vacancies can reduce Young’s modulus and stiffness, with one study reporting that defects up to 20% can decrease Young’s modulus by more than one order of magnitude [N1-F1]. Another study explicitly investigates vacancy defects in graphene by molecular dynamics simulation, showing that vacancies affect Young’s modulus and fracture behavior [N4-R5]. This means vacancies are not just local disruptions—they are major contributors to global stiffness loss.

Vacancies also act as stress concentrations and crack initiation sites. The same defective penta-graphene study notes that defects alter fracture behavior and that defects can be tuned to change mechanical and electronic properties, with defective PG being a good candidate for gas sensing [N1-F1]. This implies that vacancies weaken graphene not only by lowering modulus but also by creating localized strain and failure sites that can propagate cracks under load [N4-F2].

Defect density and location matter. The branch report on grain boundaries explains that failure strength depends on both misorientation angle and dislocation distribution, and that non-uniform distributions can significantly reduce failure strength [N4-F2]. The same principle applies broadly to defects: higher defect density and uneven placement introduce more local structural inhomogeneity, which lowers strength [N1-F1][N4-F2]. In other words, a small number of defects may be tolerable, but the same defects in clusters or at critical locations can have a large negative effect.

---

## 2) Dislocations: altering plasticity, changing yield stress/work hardening, and interacting with other defects

Dislocations affect graphene deformation and toughness by modifying the way the material accommodates strain. The branch report states that the accumulation of dislocations elevated the stress required to overcome further plastic deformation and that dislocations hindered dislocation propagation, contributing to exceptional mechanical performance [N2-R2]. At the same time, the evidence also notes that the macroscopic stress required to activate dislocations in the presence of a stress concentration is increased, indicating that dislocations can both promote and complicate plastic deformation [N2-R5].

Dislocation density changes yield stress and work hardening. The grain boundary study shows that the failure strength of graphene GBs increases with higher misorientation angles only when dislocations are uniformly distributed, but non-uniform distributions cause a significant decrease in failure strength [N4-F2]. While this is not a direct measure of yield stress in bulk graphene, it supports the broader principle that dislocation density and distribution influence the material’s resistance to failure and thus its effective strength [N4-F2]. The crystal plasticity source also notes that graphene can obstruct dislocation propagation to the adjacent metal layer, implying that dislocations can be both strain-hardening obstacles and sources of local strain hardening [N2-R1].

Dislocations also interact with other defects and grain boundaries. The grain boundary evidence explicitly states that GB failure strength depends on dislocation density and distribution, and that non-uniform distributions introduce large local tensile stresses and reduce failure strength [N4-F2]. This indicates that dislocations are not isolated: they redistribute strain, create local stress concentrations, and modify the failure mechanism near grain boundaries and other defects [N4-F2]. The broader defect engineering literature further supports the idea that structural defects can tune mechanical properties, so dislocations are part of a defect ensemble that modifies deformation behavior [N1-F1].

---

## 3) Grain boundaries: reducing intrinsic strength, increasing slip transfer, and acting as crack paths or barriers

Grain boundaries reduce intrinsic strength by introducing local structural inhomogeneity. The branch report shows that the failure strengths of graphene GBs were investigated over a range of misorientation angles, and that failure strength depends on both misorientation angle and dislocation distribution [N4-F2]. The same source states that failure strength increases with higher misorientation angles only when the dislocation distribution is uniform, but non-uniform distributions significantly decrease failure strength [N4-F2]. Another review notes that defective graphene can have elastic properties altered by defects, and that dilute defects in grain boundaries do not change elastic properties, but the failure behavior can be different [N3-R4]. Taken together, these findings show that GBs weaken graphene relative to pristine material by introducing localized weaknesses.

Grain boundaries also increase slip transfer and modify the deformation mechanism. The grain boundary study explains that the failure strength depends on the distribution of GB dislocations and that non-uniform distributions create local structural inhomogeneity, introducing large local tensile stresses [N4-F2]. It also states that the GB misorientation angle is not the only factor determining failure strength and that the interplay between dislocation density and distribution affects the failure mechanism [N4-F2]. This suggests that GBs promote slip transfer across the boundary, because the strain fields of dislocations can overlap and cancel in some configurations while creating stress concentrations in others. The same source also reports that higher misorientation angles can yield higher failure strength in uniform dislocation distributions, consistent with the idea that GBs can guide and redistribute strain rather than simply degrade it [N4-F2].

Grain boundaries can act as crack paths or barriers depending on orientation and length scale. The evidence indicates that GB orientation strongly influences failure behavior. The grain boundary study reports that failure strength increases with higher misorientation angles, but only when dislocations are uniformly distributed, and that non-uniform distributions cause a significant decrease in failure strength [N4-F2]. This means that orientation and defect distribution together determine whether the boundary is a weak path or a tough barrier. The broader defect literature also notes that grain boundaries can be engineered and that their properties depend on the surrounding structure, supporting the idea that GBs can be either crack paths or barriers depending on local conditions [N1-F1].

---

## 4) How defects are measured and interpreted in real graphene experiments

Defects are measured and interpreted using a combination of in situ TEM, AFM, SEM, and 4D STEM-in-SEM techniques. The branch report states that in situ TEM has emerged as a powerful technique for capturing dynamic deformation mechanisms, offering unparalleled dynamic details of deformation under mechanical stimuli and providing fundamental insights into deformation and failure mechanisms [N5-F3]. This is especially useful for linking defect presence to mechanical behavior because it can visualize structural evolution in real time [N5-F3].

AFM and TEM/SEM are also used to identify defects and probe their spatial distribution. The review notes that AFM, SEM, and TEM were used in three in situ microscopy techniques to study mechanical properties and nanomechanical behavior of two-dimensional materials [N5-R2]. Another source specifically states that AFM and TEM were used to examine mechanical properties and nanomechanical behavior of 2D materials, indicating that these methods can detect defects and relate them to mechanical response [N5-R2]. TEM can also be used to characterize defect sites and even induce defects in 2D materials [N5-R4], which highlights the importance of careful experimental design to distinguish real mechanical effects from measurement artifacts.

4D STEM-in-SEM is used to map defects and their orientation. The evidence shows that orientation mapping of graphene using 4D STEM-in-SEM was implemented in a scanning electron microscope, with interpretable diffraction patterns obtained from monolayer graphene using very short integration times [N6-R3]. A separate source states that orientation mapping of graphene was done using 4D STEM-in-SEM, and that such maps can reveal atomic-scale defects and their orientation [N6-R1]. This is important because defect density, orientation, and morphology can be extracted from the diffraction patterns and maps, enabling quantitative analysis of defect distribution and spatial arrangement [N6-R1][N6-R3].

Measurement uncertainty affects conclusions about mechanical effects. The evidence suggests that experimental conclusions depend on the quality of defect characterization. The in situ TEM review notes that TEM-based methods can capture dynamic microstructural evolution, but also discusses advantages and limitations of in situ TEM tests [N5-F3]. The fact that TEM can be used to induce defects as well as characterize them implies that some observed effects may be influenced by the measurement process itself rather than intrinsic material behavior [N5-R4]. Similarly, the need to distinguish between defect density, orientation, and morphology in real graphene means that weak or ambiguous defects can be misinterpreted unless the measurement approach is carefully controlled [N6-R1][N6-R3].

---

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Vacancies, dislocations, and grain boundaries all weaken or complicate graphene’s mechanical behavior in different ways:

- **Vacancies** lower Young’s modulus and stiffness, create stress concentrations and crack initiation sites, and reduce strength when density or location is unfavorable [N1-F1][N4-R5][N4-F2].
- **Dislocations** alter plasticity and strain capacity, can raise yield stress through strain hardening, and can reduce toughness by creating local tensile stresses or interacting with other defects and grain boundaries [N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-F2].
